questions.q: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), write the transpose \(A'\) and state its order.
questions.a: \(A' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) of order \(3 \times 2\). A wrong answer such as keeping the same order \(2 \times 3\) or writing \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) reveals that the student has not understood that rows become columns and the order changes from \(m \times n\) to \(n \times m\).

questions.q: Explain why \((A')' = A\) is always true for any matrix \(A\). Use the definition of transpose in your explanation.
questions.a: Transpose swaps rows and columns: \((A')_{ij} = a_{ji}\). Applying transpose again gives \(((A')')_{ij} = (A')_{ji} = a_{ij}\), which is exactly the original element. Hence \((A')' = A\). A wrong answer that merely states "it's a property" without referencing the index swap shows the student memorized the rule but does not understand the mechanism.

questions.q: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 \end{bmatrix}\). Compute \((A+B)'\) and \(A' + B'\) and verify they are equal.
questions.a: \(A+B = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 8 \\ 10 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\), so \((A+B)' = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 10 \\ 8 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\). \(A' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B' = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 7 \\ 6 & 8 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A' + B' = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 10 \\ 8 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\). They match. A common error is to add the transposes incorrectly (e.g., adding row-wise instead of element-wise) or to forget that addition is element-wise, revealing a shaky grasp of matrix addition.

questions.q: Given \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}_{2 \times 3}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 8 \\ 9 & 10 \\ 11 & 12 \end{bmatrix}_{3 \times 2}\), compute \((AB)'\) and \(B'A'\). Are they equal? What does this tell you about the order of multiplication in the transpose of a product?
questions.a: \(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 58 & 64 \\ 139 & 154 \end{bmatrix}\), so \((AB)' = \begin{bmatrix} 58 & 139 \\ 64 & 154 \end{bmatrix}\). \(B' = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 9 & 11 \\ 8 & 10 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\), \(A' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B'A' = \begin{bmatrix} 58 & 139 \\ 64 & 154 \end{bmatrix}\). They are equal. The order of multiplication reverses: \((AB)' = B'A'\). A student who computes \(A'B'\) (which is not even defined because \(A'\) is \(3 \times 2\) and \(B'\) is \(2 \times 3\)) or claims \((AB)' = A'B'\) has not internalized the reversal rule.

questions.q: A student claims that for any scalar \(k\) and matrix \(A\), \((kA)' = kA'\) is false because "the scalar should also be transposed". Evaluate this claim and explain why the student is wrong.
questions.a: The claim is false. Transpose acts only on the matrix entries; a scalar has no rows or columns to interchange. By definition, \((kA)_{ij} = k a_{ij}\), so \(((kA)')_{ij} = (kA)_{ji} = k a_{ji} = k (A')_{ij}\). Hence \((kA)' = kA'\). The student's error shows a misunderstanding that transpose is an operation on the array structure, not on the scalar multiplier.

questions.q: Construct a \(2 \times 3\) matrix \(A\) and a \(3 \times 2\) matrix \(B\) such that \((AB)' \neq A'B'\) (i.e., the product \(A'B'\) is defined but gives a different matrix). Show your work.
questions.a: Take \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \((AB)' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). \(A' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), \(A'B' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \neq (AB)'\). A student who cannot produce such a counterexample likely thinks \((AB)' = A'B'\) always holds, missing the crucial reversal of order.
